headline: America's top spy makes a quiet trip to Moscow

sources.title: CIA Director Arrives in Moscow for 'Meetings,' Reports Say (The Moscow Times)
CIA director visits Putin's Russia in talks that Trump calls 'sort of semi-routine' (Fortune)
Here's why the CIA director traveled to Russia (video, CBS News)

chunks.text: The head of the CIA, America's main [[intelligence agency]], has made a [[surprise visit]] to Russia. The agency's director {{set off}} from Washington on Sunday, August 23, {{stopped over}} in Riga, Latvia, and {{touched down}} at a Moscow airport on Tuesday. He flew on a C-17, a military [[transport plane]] usually used to carry soldiers and [[equipment]]. The trip was [[unannounced]]. It was the first visit by a CIA [[chief]] to Russia since November 2021, a few months before the war in Ukraine began.

verbs.why: Hikers set off at dawn, and ships set off from port. The CIA chief set off from Washington on a Sunday and reached Moscow two days later.

verbs.correct: To stay somewhere during a long trip
verbs.wrong: To wait for a delayed airplane
verbs.why: Travelers stop over in big airport cities like Dubai or Amsterdam on long routes. The director's plane stopped over in Riga before the final flight into Russia.
Planes touch down on the runway, and returning space capsules touch down in the desert. The C-17 touched down in Moscow on Tuesday, August 25.

chunks.text: Secret flights rarely stay secret. [[Flight trackers]] followed the plane's path across Europe, and the public data {{gave away}} the story. Within hours, the news {{came out}} in American media. Russian officials first said they knew nothing. Later, a Kremlin [[spokesman]] [[confirmed]] the visit and called it "contacts between [[security services]]." The American spy chief did not meet President Putin. Instead, he {{sat down}} with the head of Russia's foreign intelligence service, who described the talks as "nothing special."

verbs.correct: To let a secret become known
verbs.why: A nervous smile can give away a lie, and fingerprints give away a thief. Public flight data gave away a trip that was supposed to stay quiet.
The truth comes out, test results come out, and big news comes out. This story came out within hours of the landing in Moscow.

verbs.wrong: To argue in an angry way
verbs.why: Rivals sit down for peace talks, and unions sit down with company bosses. The American spy chief sat down with Russia's foreign intelligence head, not with the president.

chunks.text: In Washington, President Trump {{played down}} the trip, calling it "sort of semi-routine." Experts disagreed. They {{pointed out}} that a CIA director almost never travels to Moscow, and that such visits usually mean something serious is [[on the agenda]], like a [[warning]] or a [[negotiation]]. What did the two sides discuss? Officially, nobody will say, and both governments are keeping the details [[under wraps]]. [[Analysts]] believe the topics may have included the war in Ukraine and Russia's growing [[partnership]] with Iran.

verbs.correct: To make something seem less important
verbs.why: Politicians play down bad polls, and companies play down their losses. The president played down the trip, while experts said it was anything but routine.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To ask for more time to think
verbs.why: Teachers point out mistakes, and tour guides point out famous buildings. Experts pointed out that a CIA director almost never flies to Moscow.

chunks.text: One detail shows how unusual the moment was. Before the visit, Washington asked Ukraine to {{hold off}} on attacks against Moscow and St. Petersburg until the American [[delegation]] left, although [[strikes]] were {{carried out}} in other [[regions]]. Meanwhile, the war {{drags on}} into its fifth year, and [[peace talks]] have [[made no progress]] for months. Analysts do not expect a quick [[breakthrough]], and nobody knows if one quiet trip can help both sides {{work out}} a deal.

verbs.why: Shoppers hold off on big purchases, and coaches hold off on naming the team. Washington asked Ukraine to hold off on strikes against two Russian cities.

verbs.wrong: To cancel at the last minute
verbs.why: Scientists carry out experiments, and armies carry out orders. Ukrainian strikes were still carried out in other parts of Russia that week.
Court cases drag on, boring meetings drag on, and some wars drag on for years. This one drags on into its fifth year with no end in sight.

verbs.correct: To find a solution after effort
verbs.why: Friends work out their differences, and lawyers work out the fine details. Nobody knows if the two countries can work out a real peace deal.

mainIdea.s: America's spy chief quietly flew to Moscow and met Russian intelligence leaders, the first such visit in about five years. The trip stayed secret only until flight data revealed it.
mainIdea.why: The unannounced visit was the first by a CIA chief since 2021, and flight trackers exposed the plane's route within hours.

mainIdea.s: The head of American intelligence traveled to Russia and signed a deal ending attacks on both capitals. Officials now expect the war in Ukraine to finish before the end of winter.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nothing was signed. Ukraine only paused strikes on two cities during the visit, and peace talks remain stuck.

mainIdea.s: Russian intelligence officers secretly traveled to Washington to share information about terrorist groups. The two countries then agreed to reopen their embassies after years of silence.
mainIdea.why: The travel went the other way. An American spy chief flew to Moscow, and no embassy agreement was discussed.
